action_trace.summary: Generated 10 interview questions using 5W1H and Socratic techniques to elicit user goals (ODD scenarios, takeover preferences), pain points (objective conflicts, motion quality), and acceptance criteria (metrics, trade-off rules, validation evidence). Questions decompose the multiobjective optimization challenge and path-speed decoupling framework into concrete user needs and deployment constraints aligned with ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 requirements elicitation practices.

Generated 10 targeted interview questions using 5W1H and Socratic techniques to elicit user goals (ODD compliance, multiobjective optimization trade-offs), pain points (mode transitions, intervention response times), and acceptance criteria (boundary thresholds, priority hierarchies) for the autonomous driving system. Questions decompose complex requirements into stakeholder concerns and decision points aligned with ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 and BABOK v3 practices.

Generated 10 targeted interview questions using 5W1H and Socratic techniques to elicit stakeholder goals (ODD compliance, multiobjective trade-offs), pain points (handover safety, objective prioritization), and acceptance criteria (HMI response timing, performance metrics) for the AD system operating in urban/highway environments with path-speed decoupling.

End-user identifies critical pain points in manual fleet inefficiency and ODD monitoring gaps. Expects multiobjective motion planning (Safety/Smoothness/Speed) with robust HMI takeover mechanisms and domain-agnostic path-speed decoupling to enable reliable autonomous operations across urban and highway scenarios while maintaining passenger comfort and delivery performance.

End-user confirms three critical business requirements: (1) eliminate 15-20% efficiency losses in urban delivery through intelligent motion planning, (2) implement real-time ODD boundary monitoring with 2-second HMI warning for highway safety, and (3) achieve simultaneous optimization of safety (zero collisions), smoothness (≤0.3g), and speed (10% reduction) using decoupled path-speed planning framework.

End-user requirements center on resolving 15-20% urban delivery inefficiency through multi-objective optimization (safety/smoothness/speed) and establishing real-time ODD boundary monitoring with 2-second HMI alert response for highway logistics safety. System must enable automated decision-making while maintaining human oversight capability and operational reliability across urban and highway scenarios.

Six clarification questions raised to resolve ambiguities in multiobjective optimization arbitration, ODD boundary detection thresholds, scenario-specific constraints, path-speed decoupling implementation, driver variability scope, and ODD parameter definition for the AD autonomous delivery system.

Six critical clarification questions raised by End User to resolve ambiguities in conflicting multiobjective optimization priorities, ODD boundary monitoring thresholds, scenario-specific constraint applicability, efficiency measurement baselines, human takeover fallback behavior, and scenario definition scope. These questions directly address gaps between pain points (15-20% efficiency loss, safety incidents from ODD non-compliance) and expectations (simultaneous Safety-Smoothness-Speed optimization with 2-second HMI response).

Six critical clarification questions identified addressing priority hierarchies for conflicting objectives (Safety-Speed trade-offs), undefined ODD boundary thresholds, scenario-specific constraint applicability, mathematical feasibility of simultaneous optimization targets, HMI warning adequacy, and scenario-dependent optimization tuning. Chain-of-Thought analysis reveals ambiguities in requirement prioritization and boundary definitions that must be resolved before system design can proceed.

End user confirms core requirements for autonomous delivery systems with refined clarifications: Safety-first priority hierarchy (Safety > Smoothness > Speed), adaptive 80%-threshold ODD boundary monitoring with 2-second HMI warning latency, and uniform ≤0.3g smoothness constraint across scenarios. All pain points and expectations validated as achievable under deterministic multiobjective optimization framework.

End-user requirements validated and refined: Safety-Speed-Smoothness hierarchy established with Safety as non-negotiable priority; ODD boundary monitoring clarified with 80% adaptive thresholds and 2-second HMI warning requirement; scenario-specific smoothness constraints and conflict resolution mechanisms require further clarification before system design.

End-user has confirmed operational scenarios (urban delivery, highway logistics) and refined critical requirements: deterministic Safety > Smoothness > Speed priority hierarchy; adaptive ODD boundary detection at 80% threshold limits with 2-second HMI warning; uniform ≤0.3g lateral acceleration constraint. Safety is absolute and non-negotiable. All pain points and expectations are validated and requirement-grounded.

Consolidated 8 structured elicitation records documenting AD case requirements: operating scenarios (urban/highway), ODD boundary monitoring with 2-second HMI warning at 80% adaptive thresholds, deterministic Safety>Smoothness>Speed priority hierarchy, uniform ≤0.3g lateral acceleration constraint, 15-20% efficiency improvement target, path-speed decoupling architecture, MoSCoW prioritization (Safety=MUST), and trade-off traceability. All records align with ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 documentation standards and address enduser pain points, clarifications, and confirmations from dialogue history.

Synthesized hierarchical user requirements prioritizing safety-critical ODD monitoring (MUST) with adaptive 80% threshold-based HMI warnings, deterministic multiobjective optimization hierarchy (Safety > Smoothness > Speed), and path-speed decoupling architecture to address urban delivery efficiency gaps (15-20% loss) while maintaining ≤0.3g comfort constraint uniformly across both operational scenarios. Seven requirements derived from six interview records and validated enduser confirmations, organized by MoSCoW priority with traceability to source artifacts.

Seven targeted questions probe deployer infrastructure constraints (network, compute, sensors), security mandates (functional safety, SOTIF, fail-safe modes), and scalability expectations (hardware budgets, edge vs. cloud, geographic constraints). Questions anchor to existing requirement fragments (2-second HMI warning, 80% adaptive threshold, Safety > Smoothness > Speed hierarchy, 15-20% efficiency loss, ≤0.3g lateral acceleration) and elicit deployment-specific design decisions that bridge the gap between abstract user requirements and concrete system implementation.

Formulated seven targeted deployment-focused questions probing infrastructure latency/edge computing, cybersecurity/functional safety compliance, computational resource budgets, ODD sensor integration, operational scenario coverage, HMI integration feasibility, and efficiency validation metrics. Questions directly address constraints and enablers for implementing the Safety-Smoothness-Speed priority hierarchy, 2-second HMI warning response, and 80% adaptive threshold-based ODD boundary detection across urban and highway deployment scenarios.

Seven targeted questions probe deployer infrastructure constraints (sensor fusion, communication latency, edge computing), security-safety mandate interactions, scalability of multiobjective optimization across deployment scales, efficiency loss recovery metrics, ODD boundary monitoring operational feasibility, human takeover readiness, and scenario-specific constraint applicability. Questions apply Chain-of-Thought decomposition to bridge urban/highway operational scenarios, 2-second HMI warning requirement, path-speed decoupling framework, and 15-20% efficiency improvement target with deployment realities.

Deployer confirms infrastructure constraints (dual-tier compute with ≤50ms latency edge nodes), security mandates (cryptographic signing of ODD sensor inputs, audit logging of Safety decisions), scalability strategy (stateless path-speed decoupling for 3-5x fleet growth), and cost-mitigation phased deployment targeting highest-impact urban intersections. All requirements satisfy ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 deploy environment checklist with availability-cost-performance trade-offs documented.

Five critical operational context gaps identified in Deployer infrastructure constraints and security mandates: (1) latency-cycle-time mathematical conflict in edge computing specifications, (2) sensor spoofing response protocol undefined, (3) dual-tier compute synchronization strategy missing, (4) deployment scale and cost trade-off parameters absent, (5) ISO 29148 traceability between operational requirements and infrastructure constraints incomplete. Recommend clarification on compute architecture topology, trusted data source classification, fleet scale, and failsafe behavior before infrastructure procurement.

Six operational context gaps identified in deployer responses spanning infrastructure-security trade-offs (latency budgets for cryptographic signing), compute architecture ambiguity (dual-tier safety/smoothness separation), efficiency-cost conflicts, sensor fusion update rate reconciliation, and safety-speed arbitration rules. Requires clarification on acceptable latency/cost/performance trade-offs and deterministic resolution rules for conflicting constraints before infrastructure deployment decisions.

Five operational context gaps identified requiring deployer clarification: (1) latency-frequency mathematical inconsistency in urban edge nodes (50ms vs. ≥100Hz); (2) cryptographic signing latency impact on 2-second HMI warning deadline; (3) physical vs. logical separation of Safety/Smoothness dual-tier architecture; (4) quantitative safety margins for efficiency optimization trade-offs; (5) adaptive threshold weighting across heterogeneous ODD boundary conditions. These gaps prevent deterministic requirement allocation to deployment infrastructure and must be resolved before SRS formulation per ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148.

Deployer role confirms resolution of three critical conflicts: (1) latency vs. frequency via hierarchical processing architecture; (2) dual-tier compute separation clarified as logical with physical co-location on deterministic platform; (3) security mandate operationalized with boundary-spoofing prevention and API integrity controls. Edge deployment on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin at 8-12 nodes per corridor is cost-justified (40% TCO reduction vs. centralized). All infrastructure constraints validated; ready for SRS phase.

Deployment requirements validated and refined: 50ms ODD monitoring latency achievable through pipelined architecture independent of 100Hz safety evaluation cycle; dual-tier compute architecture clarified as logically separate, physically co-located on deterministic platform; security mandates operationalized at external ingestion boundary with internal authenticated message passing; phased edge deployment strategy recommended for cost-scalability trade-off across urban and highway scenarios; availability targets established (≥99.95% for safety, ≥99.0% for optimization tiers) per ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 deployment checklist.

Deployer role confirms deployment feasibility of AD case requirements through validated dual-tier edge computing architecture (QNX/VxWorks + Jetson AGX Orin) achieving 50ms ODD monitoring latency and ≥100Hz safety constraint evaluation. Cryptographic security applied only to external sensor ingestion boundary. Cost-performance analysis shows $12-18K capital investment for 10-15 intersection nodes with <$2K annual operational cost per site. Path-Speed Decoupling framework enables scalable extension to highway logistics scenarios without infrastructure redesign.

Comprehensive operating environment specification for autonomous delivery system (Case AD) integrating dual-scenario operations (urban congestion + highway logistics) with deterministic safety-first motion planning, adaptive ODD boundary monitoring, edge computing infrastructure (50ms latency ceiling), cryptographically-secured sensor fusion, and deterministic real-time execution (≥100Hz safety, ≤0.3g smoothness constraint, 10% speed improvement target) across physically co-located but logically separated compute tiers.

Consolidated 10-item system requirements list (IEEE 830 format) derived from user-level, environment-level, and deployment-level requirements. Establishes operational scenarios (urban/highway), ODD monitoring with 80% threshold-based HMI warnings (2-second trigger), deterministic Safety-Smoothness-Speed priority hierarchy, path-speed decoupling architecture, 15-20% efficiency improvement target, ≥100Hz safety execution, 50ms end-to-end latency ceiling, cryptographic sensor fusion security (ECDSA P-256/TLS 1.3), real-time performance monitoring, and edge computing deployment specifications. All requirements reconcile deployer constraints, enduser confirmations, and IEEE 830/ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 compliance standards.

Selected SysML (Block Definition Diagram + Internal Block Diagram + Parametric Constraints) as primary modeling methodology, supplemented by UML Use Case Diagram. SysML enables formal specification of hierarchical safety-critical architecture, multiobjective optimization constraints with deterministic priority hierarchy, and resolution of latency-frequency trade-offs across distributed edge computing deployment. UML use cases provide actor-centric traceability from enduser pain points (15-20% urban efficiency loss, highway ODD safety gaps) through system requirements. Combined approach satisfies IEEE 830 and ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 consistency and traceability requirements while explicitly addressing deployer operational context gaps and enduser clarifications through constraint formalization.

Constructed comprehensive requirements model for AD autonomous delivery system with three validated operational tiers: (1) ODD Monitoring & HMI (adaptive 80% threshold detection, 2-second warning trigger), (2) Multiobjective Motion Planning (deterministic Safety > Smoothness > Speed hierarchy with path-speed decoupling), (3) Infrastructure & Security (50ms end-to-end latency on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, cryptographic signing at sensor ingestion boundary). Chain-of-Thought analysis resolved three critical conflicts: latency-frequency trade-off (50ms ceiling vs. ≥100Hz safety evaluation), dual-tier architecture clarification (logically separate, physically co-located cores), and safety-speed priority hierarchy (Safety non-negotiable, Speed constrained to 10% improvement). All enduser clarifications closed, deployer questions operationalized, and consistency verified against IEEE 830 and ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 standards. No unresolved gaps remain in requirement model.
